Virginia in 1790

1790 census: 747,610 people, 292,627 of them enslaved (39.1%).

Counted for the House under the three-fifths clause: 630,559. That gave Virginia 19 House seats in 1793 (one for every 33,000 people), plus 2 senators, like every state.

If enslaved people had been counted in full: 22 seats. If they had not been counted at all: 13 seats.

Virginia's census figure excludes Kentucky, which was counted separately. Today's state outlines, with Maine shown as part of Massachusetts and West Virginia as part of Virginia, as they were in the 1790s.

Seats: National Archives · Ratio: U.S. Census Bureau

North Carolina: 12th state to ratify

Ratified on November 21, 1789: 194 for, 77 against.

The convention met at the State House, Fayetteville, 16–23 November 1789.

A first convention, at Hillsborough in 1788, voted 184 to 83 against ratifying.

Delaware: 1st state to ratify

Ratified on December 7, 1787: 30 for, 0 against.

The convention met at the Golden Fleece Tavern, Dover, 3–7 December 1787.

results.popup:
New Orleans

January 8, 1815 

Where: Louisiana (today's name)

US victory 

Total Casualties: 2,096 
____________________________________________________

The United States achieved its greatest land victory of the War of 1812 at New Orleans. The battle ended a British effort to gain control of a critical American port and elevated Maj. Gen. Andrew Jackson to national fame. The British launched a forward attack against American forces at Chalmette Plantation. British casualties far outnumbered those of the Americans. Jackson's fame from the battle contributed to him winning the presidential election thirteen years later.

The British strategy had been to focus on attacking American coastal regions to cripple American trade and transportation. Although they had been unable to take Baltimore, the British moved ahead with a plan to attack New Orleans.

The Americans were aware of a possible invasion on the Gulf Coast. Andrew Jackson reached the city on December 1 and began assembling an army. His force consisted of Tennessee and Kentucky frontiersmen, Louisiana militia, New Orleans businessmen, free men of color, Choctaw warriors, smuggler Jean Lafitte and his privateers, sailors, marines, and United States troops.

On January 8, 1815, Maj. Gen. Andrew Jackson's hastily assembled army won the day against a battle-hardened and numerically superior British force. The resounding American victory at the Battle of New Orleans soon became a symbol of American democracy triumphing over the old European ideas of aristocracy and entitlement. The battle was the last major armed engagement between the United States and Britain.

Pennsylvania in 1796: 15 electors

In the pie: John Adams (Federalist), 1 vote; Thomas Jefferson (Democratic-Republican), 14 votes.

All electors' votes in 1796: John Adams 1, Thomas Jefferson 14, Thomas Pinckney 2, Aaron Burr 13. Each elector cast two votes for president, so the votes add up to twice the number of electors.

Today's state outlines, with Maine shown as part of Massachusetts and West Virginia as part of Virginia, as they were in the 1790s.

Source: National Archives

Virginia in 1796: 21 electors

In the pie: John Adams (Federalist), 1 vote; Thomas Jefferson (Democratic-Republican), 20 votes.

All electors' votes in 1796: John Adams 1, Thomas Jefferson 20, Thomas Pinckney 1, Aaron Burr 1, Samuel Adams 15, others 4. Each elector cast two votes for president, so the votes add up to twice the number of electors.

The National Archives' 1800 table shows a dash (no votes) for Virginia's Aaron Burr, but its own Burr total of 73 needs Virginia's 21. Today's state outlines, with Maine shown as part of Massachusetts and West Virginia as part of Virginia, as they were in the 1790s.

Source: National Archives

Pennsylvania in 1800: 15 electors

In the pie: John Adams (Federalist), 7 votes; Thomas Jefferson (Democratic-Republican), 8 votes.

All electors' votes in 1800: Thomas Jefferson 8, Aaron Burr 8, John Adams 7, Charles C. Pinckney 7. Each elector cast two votes for president, so the votes add up to twice the number of electors.

Jefferson and Aaron Burr tied with 73 votes each, so the House of Representatives chose the president: Jefferson, on 17 February 1801. The 12th Amendment (1804) then gave electors separate votes for president and vice president.

Today's state outlines, with Maine shown as part of Massachusetts and West Virginia as part of Virginia, as they were in the 1790s.

Source: National Archives
